Turnt
TURNT
adjective (Millennial slang)
A dialect past participle of turn (turned up → turnt up → turnt), from Southern and Atlanta hip-hop of the late 2000s, where turn up meant to get wild at a party. It spread across Twitter and Vine from about 2012; the 2013 club hit "Turn Down for What" (DJ Snake and Lil Jon) made the attitude a national chant. Turnt covers a range from hyped and energetic to thoroughly drunk or high ("turnt up," "too turnt"). Its opposite, turnt down, means calmed or sober.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

To be turnt is to be at full party intensity: loud, wild, uninhibited, and in most usage intoxicated. "Getting turnt" is the plan for a Friday night; "too turnt" is the state in which one regrets the photos the next morning. The Christian observation: the word sometimes means only high spirits, but its centre of gravity is drunkenness, and Scripture names that plainly. "And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit" (Eph 5:18). "Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise" (Pro 20:1). The prophets pronounced woe on the culture of the all-night party: "Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!" (Isa 5:11). Peter told new believers that the old life of "excess of wine, revellings, banquetings" had lasted long enough (1Pe 4:3). The deeper point is in Ephesians: the turnt state is a counterfeit filling. Men drink to be lifted out of themselves, freed from fear, loosened into joy. The Spirit gives the real thing, and it leaves a man more himself, not less. A father tells his son: you will be offered a night of being turnt in exchange for your judgment; it is a bad trade every time. Learn to have a great time sober, and you will remember your best nights.

Webster 1828 Definition

Millennial hip-hop slang (late 2000s; mainstream 2012–2014) for party-wild, usually intoxicated; Scripture calls it drunkenness and offers the true filling: be not drunk with wine, but be filled with the Spirit (Eph 5:18). Reject.

TURNT, adj. (Millennial slang, late 2000s–2010s; dialect past participle of turn up) Wildly excited; partying hard; often drunk or high. "We got turnt." Also turnt up; opposite turnt down.

Decode for parents: "getting turnt" almost always means drinking; ask the plain question.

Key Scripture

Eph 5:18 — "And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit;"

Pro 20:1 — "Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise."

Isa 5:11 — "Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!"

1Pe 4:3 — "For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries:"

Pro 23:31-32 — "Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it moveth itself aright. At the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder."

Modern Corruption

Turnt makes intoxication the goal of a good night; Scripture calls it excess and offers the Spirit’s filling, which brings joy without the loss of self.

expand to see more

The corruption is that the word makes the loss of control the point. A party is judged by how turnt it got; the stories told afterward are about who lost the most judgment. Proverbs describes the progression with uncomfortable precision: "Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it moveth itself aright. At the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder" (Pro 23:31-32). The night that begins as fun ends with someone in a ditch, in a bed they regret, or in a cell.

The recovery is not a joyless refusal but a better fullness. Paul sets drunkenness and the Spirit side by side because both promise to lift a man beyond himself; only one keeps the promise. The Spirit-filled life overflows in "speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord" (Eph 5:19), and the joy is still there in the morning. Teach the young that sobriety is not boredom, that the best celebrations in Scripture were feasts before the Lord, and that a clear head is a gift to their future selves.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English turnian (Latin tornare, to turn on a lathe) → turn up → Southern hip-hop turnt (up) → 2013 "Turn Down for What."
